title: CHARA Array Observations of the Evolved Components in Symbiotic Star Systems
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal (ApJ)
summary: The nature of the mechanisms that drive mass transfer in symbiotic stars remains an area of active research in stellar astronomy. Constraining the role that both stellar winds and Roche-lobe overflow play in this process is crucial to improving our understanding of these binaries and connecting them to important transient events such as recurrent novae and Type Ia supernovae. The high-resolution capabilities of an optical interferometer can resolve the geometric structure of the red giant in symbiotic stars and help answer this question. This work presents the results of an optical interferometric study using the Center for High Angular Resolution Astronomy (CHARA) Array for the purpose of measuring the angular diameter of and imaging the cool giant in four symbiotic and related systems. Here we report \textit{H} band observations collected with MIRC-X. Model fitting and image reconstruction are used to test for Roche-lobe-filling geometries. Near-simultaneous infrared spectroscopy taken using the NASA InfraRed Telescope Facility (IRTF) is used to determine the fundamental stellar parameters of the cool giant in each system. The parametric fits reported here favor circularly symmetric disk models over elongated geometries, while imaging suggests the presence of surface features on three of these stars. We find that the three systems with constrained orbits have inferred time-averaged filling factors below unity.

AI.tldr: This paper uses high-resolution optical interferometry with the CHARA Array and MIRC-X to measure angular diameters and image cool giants in four symbiotic star systems, finding circularly symmetric disk geometries favored over Roche-lobe-filling elongated shapes, with time-averaged filling factors below unity for the three systems with constrained orbits.
AI.motivation: The mechanisms driving mass transfer in symbiotic stars (stellar winds vs. Roche-lobe overflow) remain poorly understood, and constraining these is essential for connecting symbiotic binaries to recurrent novae and Type Ia supernovae. Measuring the geometric structure of the red giant can help resolve this question.
AI.method: The study uses the CHARA Array optical interferometer with the MIRC-X instrument in H band to measure angular diameters and image the cool giants in four symbiotic and related systems. Parametric model fitting and image reconstruction are used to test for Roche-lobe-filling geometries, while near-simultaneous IRTF infrared spectroscopy is used to determine fundamental stellar parameters.
AI.result: Parametric fits favor circularly symmetric disk models over elongated geometries, while imaging reveals surface features on three of the four stars. The three systems with constrained orbits have inferred time-averaged filling factors below unity, indicating the cool giants do not fill their Roche lobes on average.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest that the cool giants in these symbiotic systems are not Roche-lobe-filling on average, implying that stellar wind mass transfer is the likely dominant mechanism. This has implications for understanding mass transfer in symbiotic binaries and their connection to transient events like recurrent novae and Type Ia supernovae.

title: BSN-VIII: Detailed Photometric Modeling of Ten W UMa Contact Binaries and a Revised Empirical Period-Mass Relationship
summary: This study continues our ongoing research on contact binary systems by presenting a detailed analysis of 10 targets. Ground-based observations from six different observatories were conducted and used together with TESS data for the analysis process. Photometric data from our observations were reduced with the recently developed AutoWISP pipeline, yielding high-quality light curves with reliable precision for analysis. An investigation of orbital period variations identifies long-term trends in six of the ten analyzed binaries, including three that also display cyclic variations. Four targets show essentially constant orbital periods. The secular trends are attributed to mass transfer. The cyclic modulations in three systems are caused by either magnetic activity cycles or the Light-Travel Time Effect (LTTE) of a third body, while that in the remaining system is solely due to the LTTE. The BSN application was used to model the photometric light curves of the 10 target binaries. Iterative fitting and MCMC refinement provided robust estimates of the system parameters, while starspot modeling was applied for systems showing O'Connell-effect asymmetries. We refine the empirical orbital period-mass relationship for short-period contact binaries by analyzing a homogeneous dataset of systems and deriving an updated primary-mass calibration based on the spectroscopic subset. Using this calibrated relation, the fundamental parameters of the studied systems were subsequently estimated.

AI.tldr: This study presents a detailed analysis of 10 contact binary systems using ground-based observations from six observatories combined with TESS space data. Using the AutoWISP pipeline for photometric reduction and BSN modeling with MCMC refinement, the authors identify orbital period variations (6 with secular trends, 3 with cyclic modulations) and estimate system parameters, including an updated empirical orbital period-mass relationship for short-period contact binaries.
AI.motivation: To continue ongoing research on contact binary systems by providing detailed photometric and period variation analyses of 10 targets, and to refine the empirical orbital period-mass relationship for short-period contact binaries using a homogeneous dataset.
AI.method: Ground-based photometric observations from six observatories were combined with TESS data. The AutoWISP pipeline was used for data reduction. Orbital period variation analysis identified secular and cyclic trends. The BSN application was used for light curve modeling with iterative fitting and MCMC refinement, including starspot modeling for systems with O'Connell-effect asymmetries.
AI.result: Six of ten binaries show long-term orbital period trends (attributed to mass transfer), three of which also display cyclic variations (from magnetic activity or LTTE), while four show constant periods. The updated period-mass calibration enabled estimation of fundamental parameters for all systems.
AI.conclusion: The study provides refined system parameters for 10 contact binaries and updates the empirical orbital period-mass relationship for short-period contact binaries, improving the accuracy of fundamental parameter estimation for such systems.

title: Spectral Synthesis for Classical Ae Stars: H$α$ and CaII
comment: 18 pages, 13 figures and 3 tables. Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Classical Ae stars (CAe) are main sequence, A-type stars with H$α$ emission but no signature of dust; they are thought to be the cool extension of the classical Be (CBe) stars to lower stellar masses. We investigate the use of H$α$ and the CaII IR triplet observed at low spectroscopic resolution ($R=1800$) as diagnostics for the circumstellar disks of the CAe stars. Using a sample of 159 CAe stars from the LAMOST survey (DR5), we find that circumstellar disk masses and star/disk viewing inclination angles can be reliably determined from low resolution H$α$ profiles. The CAe disk mass distribution agrees well with the previous range found for late-type CBe stars, although there is an apparent increase in disk mass for the latest CAe spectral sub-types (A3 and A4) which we attribute to selection effects. Over the spectral range A2 through B6, the average disk-to-star mass ratio for the CAe and CBe stars is consistent with $\log_{10}(M_{\rm disk}/M_*)=-9.1$. A minority of the CAe sample ($\sim$16%) also show emission in the CaII IR triplet. The observed emission is well within the range predicted by the disk models, and there is statistical evidence that the CaII emitters have systematically larger H$α$ disk masses.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates classical Ae (CAe) stars—main sequence A-type stars with Hα emission but no dust—as the cool extension of classical Be (CBe) stars. Using low-resolution spectroscopy (R=1800) of 159 CAe stars from LAMOST DR5, the authors demonstrate that circumstellar disk masses and viewing inclination angles can be reliably derived from Hα profiles. Disk mass distributions agree with late-type CBe stars, with an average disk-to-star mass ratio of log10(M_disk/M_*)=−9.1 across A2 to B6, and ~16% of the sample shows CaII IR triplet emission correlated with larger disk masses.
AI.motivation: To test whether low-resolution spectroscopy can serve as a reliable diagnostic for circumstellar disks around classical Ae stars, extending the well-studied classical Be star disk diagnostics to lower stellar masses.
AI.method: Analysis of 159 CAe stars from the LAMOST DR5 survey at low spectral resolution (R=1800), using Hα line profiles to derive disk masses and viewing inclination angles, and examining CaII IR triplet emission as an additional disk diagnostic. Results are compared to disk models and to CBe star disk properties.
AI.result: Disk masses and inclinations are reliably determined from low-resolution Hα profiles. CAe disk masses match late-type CBe stars, though latest spectral sub-types (A3–A4) show higher masses attributed to selection effects. The average disk-to-star mass ratio across A2–B6 is log10(M_disk/M_*)=−9.1. About 16% of CAe stars show CaII IR triplet emission, which is consistent with model predictions and statistically associated with systematically larger Hα disk masses.
AI.conclusion: Low-resolution Hα spectroscopy is an effective tool for studying CAe circumstellar disks, confirming CAe stars as the low-mass extension of CBe stars. The disk properties scale consistently across the B to A spectral range, with CaII emission serving as a tracer of more massive disks.

title: A 500 pc volume-limited sample of hot subluminous stars III. The short-period binary population
summary: Hot subdwarf stars of spectral types O and B (sdO/B) in binaries form as products of substantial mass loss near the tip of the red giant branch and offer powerful constraints on binary-star evolutionary models. However, details of some formation channels remain missing. We present a comprehensive analysis of the short-period binary population in the 500 pc volume-limited sample of hot subdwarfs, enabled by precise Gaia DR3 parallaxes. Besides 45 known binaries within 500 pc, this work identifies 50 new single-lined radial-velocity variable systems, 34 with orbital solutions with periods between 0.07 and 22 days. We derive an overall short-period binary fraction of 34.7 (+2.8/-2.9)% for the full sample of 301 hot subdwarfs within 500 pc, corrected for orbital inclination and detection efficiency. The newly solved binaries predominantly occupy the 1-20 day range, a parameter space previously under-represented in the literature. We identify five new reflection-effect systems, three ellipsoidal modulation systems, a newly solved HW Vir system, and a new triple candidate. The sdB and sdO binary fractions are similar, while the sdOB class shows a fraction roughly half that of sdB/sdO stars, with periods over one day, suggesting a different evolutionary pathway. Underluminous hot subdwarfs below the canonical extreme horizontal branch show a binary fraction comparable to other sdB/sdO stars but host only white dwarf companions, which are more massive and mainly found at periods under one day. We provide the first volume-complete birthrate estimates for sub-populations, determining a Galactic merger rate of 2.5+-1.5x10^-5 yr^-1 for sdO/B binaries, explaining no more than ~12% of the eHe-sdO population. We also derive birthrates for two SN Ia progenitor channels, finding hot subdwarf binaries could account for up to 2.5 (+0.7/-0.5)% of the observed Galactic SN Ia rate.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of short-period hot subdwarf (sdO/B) binaries within 500 pc using Gaia DR3 parallaxes, identifying 50 new radial-velocity variable systems (34 with orbital solutions, periods 0.07-22 days). The overall short-period binary fraction is 34.7% for the full sample of 301 hot subdwarfs. The authors find sdO/B binary fractions are similar, sdOB stars have roughly half the binary fraction with periods over one day, and underluminous hot subdwarfs host only white dwarf companions at short periods. They provide volume-complete birthrate estimates, determining a Galactic merger rate of 2.5×10⁻⁵ yr⁻¹ for sdO/B binaries (explaining ≤12% of eHe-sdO population) and finding hot subdwarf binaries could account for up to 2.5% of observed Galactic SN Ia rates.
AI.motivation: Hot subdwarf stars in binaries form through substantial mass loss near the tip of the red giant branch and provide powerful constraints on binary evolutionary models, yet details of some formation channels remain missing. A volume-limited sample enabled by precise Gaia DR3 parallaxes offers the opportunity to statistically constrain these channels.
AI.method: The study analyzes the complete 500 pc volume-limited sample of 301 hot subdwarfs using Gaia DR3 astrometry, with radial-velocity monitoring to identify binaries. They employ orbital solutions, correction for orbital inclination and detection efficiency, and derive binary fractions for sub-populations. Birthrate estimates are computed using the volume-complete nature of the sample, including merger rates and SN Ia progenitor channel contributions.
AI.result: 50 new single-lined radial-velocity variable systems were identified, 34 with orbital solutions (0.07-22 day periods). The short-period binary fraction is 34.7% (+2.8/-2.9)% for the full sample. Newly solved binaries cluster in the 1-20 day period range. Five new reflection-effect systems, three ellipsoidal modulation systems, a newly solved HW Vir system, and a new triple candidate were identified. The sdB and sdO binary fractions are similar, sdOB shows roughly half the fraction, and underluminous subdwarfs host only white dwarf companions. The Galactic merger rate is 2.5±1.5×10⁻⁵ yr⁻¹, explaining ≤12% of eHe-sdO, and hot subdwarf binaries could account for up to 2.5% of the observed SN Ia rate.
AI.conclusion: The volume-limited sample provides statistically robust binary fractions that reveal distinct evolutionary pathways among hot subdwarf sub-populations: sdOB stars follow a different channel than sdB/sdO stars, while underluminous objects exclusively harbor white dwarf companions. The birthrate estimates constrain the contribution of hot subdwarf binaries to eHe-sdO mergers and SN Ia progenitors, showing they are a minor but non-negligible source for both.

title: Quiescent and Interacting Compact Remnant Binary Populations in the Space Telescope Era
comment: Submitted to PASA on 28/08/2026. Posted to arXiv so that predictions for Roman's Galactic Bulge survey are available pre-launch. Synthetic populations will be made available on the BPASS website upon paper acceptance, until then request directly from the authors. The authors also welcome comments
summary: Since the discovery of Gaia BH1, interest in quiescent binary systems has grown. Two additional black-hole binaries have since been discovered alongside several candidate neutron-star binaries, yet the formation pathways of these systems remain poorly understood. Theoretical studies of these systems, together with the populations into which they evolve, such as X-ray binaries (XRBs), can help constrain their formation channels. We present predictions for the Galactic population of quiescent binary systems and their later evolutionary phases, including XRBs and post-interaction quiescent binaries. We combine stellar models from the Binary Population and Spectral Synthesis code (BPASS) with a synthetic Milky Way generated using Feedback In Realistic Environments (FIRE) simulations. We compare our results with existing observations to assess how well the synthetic population reproduces the observations. We find generally good agreement, with observed donor masses, compact-object masses, and orbital periods largely reproduced, except for the Gaia BH systems. Our results also suggest that some accreting compact remnants with low-mass donors and wide orbital periods may not be X-ray bright. Remaining discrepancies indicate that the BPASS initial parameter space should be expanded, the common-envelope evolution prescription revised, and magnetic braking included in low-mass donor models. We also predict the number of systems detectable in future Gaia data releases and by the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope (hereafter referred to as Roman). In particular, the Galactic Bulge Time Domain Survey is expected to yield a significant population of quiescent black-hole binaries. We predict that ~200-600 candidate quiescent binary systems will be detected in the Galactic Bulge Time Domain Survey, while ~2500-4000 candidate systems will be identified in Gaia DR5.

AI.tldr: This study combines BPASS stellar models with FIRE-based synthetic Milky Way simulations to predict the Galactic population of quiescent binary systems and their evolutionary descendants (XRBs and post-interaction binaries). The synthetic population generally reproduces observed donor masses, compact-object masses, and orbital periods, except for Gaia BH systems. The paper also predicts ~200-600 candidate quiescent binaries detectable in Roman's Galactic Bulge Time Domain Survey and ~2500-4000 in Gaia DR5.
AI.motivation: Following the discovery of Gaia BH1 and additional black-hole/neutron-star binaries, the formation pathways of quiescent binary systems remain poorly understood. Theoretical modeling of these systems and their descendant populations (e.g., XRBs) is needed to constrain their formation channels.
AI.method: The authors combine Binary Population and Spectral Synthesis (BPASS) stellar models with a synthetic Milky Way generated using Feedback In Realistic Environments (FIRE) simulations. They then compare the synthetic binary populations against existing observations to validate their model.
AI.result: The synthetic population shows generally good agreement with observations for donor masses, compact-object masses, and orbital periods, except for the Gaia BH systems. The model predicts some accreting compact remnants with low-mass donors and wide orbits may not be X-ray bright. Forecasts yield ~200-600 candidate quiescent binaries for the Roman Galactic Bulge Time Domain Survey and ~2500-4000 for Gaia DR5.
AI.conclusion: Remaining discrepancies suggest expansions to the BPASS initial parameter space, a revised common-envelope evolution prescription, and inclusion of magnetic braking in low-mass donor models. The study provides concrete predictions for upcoming observational surveys, particularly highlighting the Roman Galactic Bulge Time Domain Survey as a promising avenue to detect a significant population of quiescent black-hole binaries.

title: Dynamically driven collapse of a thermally stable accretion disk in a nova-like system
summary: While standard disk instability theory predicts thermal-steady, outburst-free disks in nova-like variables due to their high mass transfer rates, mass transfer variations are prevailingly invoked to explain the occasional flaring/fading phenomena observed in these systems. Here we report the observational evidence for a dynamical collapse of a thermally stable accretion disk, captured serendipitously by TESS during a fading episode of the VY Scl-type nova-like system MASTER OT J072703.91-631952.8, and traced by the emergence of an unusual negative superhump that evolves toward its orbital frequency. Simultaneously, the system underwent an anomalous eruptive event featuring a remarkably symmetric 45-day light-curve profile, indicative of a mild energy-release mechanism fundamentally distinct from documented eruptive events in cataclysmic variables. Notably, the concurrence of the eruption and the disk collapse is difficult to reconcile with the paradigm of mass transfer variations: the eruption implies enhanced mass transfer, whereas the disk collapse indicates a decline. The morphological disk evolution over $\sim 700$ days, characterized by both negative and positive superhumps, indicates a transition from a circular disk to an eccentric disk, followed by a tilted state and ultimately a minimal disk configuration. This evolutionary sequence provides evidence for a previously unrecognized dynamics-driven cycle operating in the thermally stable accretion disk of a VY Scl-type nova-like star.

AI.tldr: The paper reports TESS observations of a VY Scl-type nova-like system (MASTER OT J072703.91-631952.8) revealing a dynamical collapse of a thermally stable accretion disk, accompanied by an anomalous symmetric 45-day eruption and a transition from circular to eccentric to tilted disk states via superhump evolution. This challenges the mass-transfer-variation paradigm and suggests a dynamics-driven cycle in thermally stable disks.
AI.motivation: Standard disk instability theory predicts outburst-free, thermally steady disks in nova-like variables with high mass transfer rates, yet flaring/fading events are typically attributed to mass transfer variations. The authors aim to test this paradigm using serendipitous TESS observations of a fading episode and eruptive event in a VY Scl-type system.
AI.method: Analysis of TESS photometric time-series data over ~700 days, tracing superhump evolution (negative and positive), the emergence of a negative superhump converging toward the orbital frequency, the light-curve morphology of an eruptive event, and the morphological evolution of the accretion disk.
AI.result: The system exhibited a dynamical collapse of a thermally stable accretion disk concurrent with an anomalous symmetric 45-day eruption. The contradiction between the eruption (implying enhanced mass transfer) and disk collapse (implying decline) is inconsistent with mass transfer variations. Superhump evolution revealed a sequence from circular to eccentric to tilted to minimal disk configurations, indicating a novel dynamics-driven cycle.
AI.conclusion: The observations provide evidence for a previously unrecognized dynamics-driven cycle operating in thermally stable accretion disks of VY Scl-type nova-like stars, fundamentally different from predictions of standard disk instability theory and the mass-transfer-variation paradigm.

title: A decade of radial-velocity monitoring of rho Leo: moment analysis and periodic variability
comment: 33 pages, 19 figures, 5 tables. Accepted for publication in Universe
summary: We investigate the origin of long-term spectroscopic and photometric variability in the blue supergiant rho Leo, with particular emphasis on distinguishing between intrinsic pulsations and variability induced by a possible companion. Our analysis is based on an 11.5-year spectroscopic time series obtained at Tartu Observatory, complemented by high-cadence, high-resolution spectroscopy from the Hertzsprung SONG telescope and space-based photometry from TESS. We studied line-profile variability using normalised moments of the HeI 6678, HeI 5875, and SiIII 4552 lines. Periodic signals were identified using the generalised Lomb-Scargle periodogram with iterative pre-whitening, and their temporal stability was examined with the weighted wavelet Z-transform. We detect a persistent periodic signal at P = 16.46 d in the first and third moments, present throughout the full observing interval, with a radial-velocity amplitude of 3.9 km/s. This signal is also present in the SONG data and is visible in multiple spectral lines, indicating a global origin. Photometric observations reveal a dominant variability timescale near 33 d, approximately twice the spectroscopic period. The stable 16.46-day period, present throughout the entire observing interval, most likely results from non-radial pulsations of the supergiant. A binary origin of the signal is not excluded, but distinguishing between these scenarios is complicated by the supergiant's complex variability pattern.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes 11.5 years of spectroscopic and photometric data of the blue supergiant rho Leo to distinguish between intrinsic pulsations and companion-induced variability. A persistent 16.46-day periodic signal is detected across multiple spectral lines and throughout the entire observing window, most likely originating from non-radial pulsations, though a binary origin cannot be fully excluded.
AI.motivation: The goal is to determine the physical origin of long-term variability in the blue supergiant rho Leo, specifically whether it arises from intrinsic stellar pulsations or from the influence of a possible companion star.
AI.method: The study combines an 11.5-year spectroscopic time series from Tartu Observatory with high-cadence spectroscopy from the Hertzsprung SONG telescope and space-based TESS photometry. Line-profile variability is analyzed using normalized moments of HeI 6678, HeI 5875, and SiIII 4552 lines. Periodic signals are identified via the generalized Lomb-Scargle periodogram with iterative pre-whitening, and temporal stability is assessed using the weighted wavelet Z-transform.
AI.result: A persistent 16.46-day period is detected in the first and third line-profile moments, present throughout the full observing interval with a radial-velocity amplitude of 3.9 km/s. This signal also appears in SONG data and across multiple spectral lines, indicating a global origin. Photometry shows a dominant timescale near 33 days, roughly double the spectroscopic period.
AI.conclusion: The stable 16.46-day period most likely originates from non-radial pulsations of the supergiant. A binary origin is not excluded, but the supergiant's complex variability makes distinguishing between these scenarios difficult.

title: CoBiToM project. III. Physical characterisation of the potential merger candidates AL Lep, ASAS J082243+1927.0, and ZZ PsA
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics journal
summary: Contact binaries (CBs) are key systems for investigating the late evolutionary stages that may lead to stellar coalescence. Systems with an extremely low mass ratio and high fill-out factor are of particular interest as potential merger candidates and possible progenitors of luminous red novae. A combined photometric and spectroscopic study of the CB systems AL Lep, ASAS J082243+1927.0, and ZZ PsA is presented. The aim is to derive self-consistent orbital and physical parameters, assess their evolutionary state, and examine whether they have reached the terminal and unstable phase of their evolution. High-resolution VLT/UVES spectra were analysed to derive radial velocity values, spectroscopic mass ratio, and metallicity. The results were combined with multi-band light-curve modelling within a Monte Carlo framework to determine the system geometries and absolute parameters. Orbital period variations were investigated through O-C analysis, while the evolutionary status of the systems was assessed using the Darwin instability criterion, critical mass ratio estimates, fill-out factor, and orbital period variation. Mass ratio values of q = 0.1332, 0.1041, and 0.0789 were derived for AL Lep, ASAS J082243+1927.0, and ZZ PsA, respectively. The corresponding primary mass values are M1 = 1.656 +/- 0.081 Msun, 1.275 +/- 0.078 Msun, and 1.795 +/- 0.111 Msun. The locations of their components show significant deviations from single-star ZAMS and TAMS reference curves, indicating strong binary interaction and energy redistribution through the common envelope. The spin-to-orbital angular momentum ratio for AL Lep and ASAS J082243+1927.0 remains below the standard Darwin instability threshold, while ZZ PsA lies close to the instability regime and may be consistent with an unstable configuration within the derived uncertainties.

AI.tldr: A combined photometric and spectroscopic study of three contact binaries (AL Lep, ASAS J082243+1927.0, and ZZ PsA) using VLT/UVES spectra and multi-band light-curve modeling to derive orbital and physical parameters, assess evolutionary states, and evaluate whether they have reached terminal unstable phases potentially leading to stellar merger.
AI.motivation: Contact binaries with extremely low mass ratios and high fill-out factors are key merger candidates and possible progenitors of luminous red novae. Studying such systems helps understand late-stage binary evolution and stellar coalescence.
AI.method: High-resolution VLT/UVES spectroscopy for radial velocities, mass ratios, and metallicities; multi-band light-curve modeling within a Monte Carlo framework for geometric and absolute parameters; O-C analysis for period variations; Darwin instability criterion and critical mass ratio estimates for evolutionary assessment.
AI.result: Mass ratios of q=0.1332, 0.1041, and 0.0789 for AL Lep, ASAS J082243+1927.0, and ZZ PsA respectively. Primary masses of M1=1.656, 1.275, and 1.795 Msun. Component locations deviate significantly from single-star ZAMS/TAMS curves. AL Lep and ASAS J082243+1927.0 have spin-to-orbital angular momentum ratios below the Darwin instability threshold, while ZZ PsA lies near the instability regime and may be consistent with unstable configuration within uncertainties.
AI.conclusion: All three systems show strong binary interaction and energy redistribution through the common envelope. ZZ PsA is the most promising merger candidate among the three, potentially approaching the terminal unstable phase, while AL Lep and ASAS J082243+1927.0 have not yet reached the Darwin instability threshold.

title: Extremely Low Mass Ratio Contact Binaries. III. Photometric and Spectroscopic Investigations of Eleven Systems
comment: 20 pages, 7 figures, 7 tables, accepted by ApJ
summary: We present photometric and spectroscopic investigations of 11 totally eclipsing contact binaries with mass ratios below 0.15, classifying them as extremely low mass ratio contact binaries. The ground-based multiband light curves were modeled with PHysics Of Eclipsing BinariEs to derive the photometric parameters of these systems. The TESS light curves of J011323 and J002747 show pronounced asymmetries and continuous variations. Markov Chain Monte Carlo modeling suggests that these variations are related to longitudinal migration of spots on the primary components. Spectral subtraction of the LAMOST spectra reveals excess chromospheric emission in six systems, while no detectable excess emission is found in the other five. The O$-$C analysis indicates secular period increases in six systems and secular decreases in five systems. We estimated their orbital angular momenta and performed a dynamical analysis. {Within our adopted semi-analytical framework without energy transfer, the formation of these observed systems requires additional angular momentum loss beyond saturated magnetic braking and gravitational radiation, but this requirement could be modified by different assumptions on mass transfer or radius evolution.

AI.tldr: The paper presents photometric and spectroscopic analyses of 11 extremely low mass ratio contact binaries (q<0.15), using ground-based multiband light curves, TESS data, and LAMOST spectra. It derives photometric parameters, detects spot-induced variations in two systems, finds chromospheric excess emission in six systems, analyzes O-C period changes, and conducts dynamical analysis showing that additional angular momentum loss beyond standard mechanisms is required for their formation.
AI.motivation: To characterize extremely low mass ratio contact binaries, understand their evolutionary status, and investigate the dynamical processes (particularly angular momentum loss and merger scenarios) governing their formation and evolution.
AI.method: Ground-based multiband light curve modeling with PHysics Of Eclipsing BinariEs (PHOEBE); analysis of TESS light curves for asymmetries (J011323 and J002747) with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) spot modeling; spectral subtraction of LAMOST spectra to detect chromospheric excess emission; O-C (observed-minus-calculated) period analysis; orbital angular momentum estimation and dynamical analysis within a semi-analytical framework.
AI.result: Photometric parameters derived for all 11 systems; spot migration on primary components explains TESS light curve variations in two systems; six systems show chromospheric excess emission; six show secular period increases and five decreases; dynamical analysis indicates the formation requires additional angular momentum loss beyond saturated magnetic braking and gravitational radiation (though this depends on mass transfer or radius evolution assumptions).
AI.conclusion: Extremely low mass ratio contact binaries require enhanced angular momentum loss mechanisms for their formation, although the exact requirement is model-dependent. The presence of spots, chromospheric activity, and diverse period changes indicates active evolutionary processes in these systems, which are potential merger candidates.

title: On the theoretical instability strips of γ-Doradus stars including the effect of the metallicity and rotation
summary: Recent space missions such as Kepler have provided large-scale observations of the γ-Doradus instability strips (IS), which can be used to constrain models and explore their limitations. One persistent limitation is the prediction of the blue edge of the γ- Doradus IS, where a significant number of γ-Doradus stars are observed. Despite these observational advances, no systematic study has been undertaken to explore the effects of different physical processes on the γ-Doradus. Our aim is to systematically explore the theoretical γ-Doradus IS with modern tools, accounting for the effects of rotation and metallicity, providing a large grid of models and their oscillation parameters for the scientific community. We investigated the non-adiabatic pulsation properties of stars in a grid of stellar models with masses between 1.35 M{_\odot} and 2.5 M{_\odot}, metallicities between Z= 0.01 and Z= 0.025, and solid-body rotation rates ranging from Ω = 0 to 0.5 {Ω_{crit}}, where {Ω_{crit}} denotes the critical rotation rate. We find that, across all computations, the theoretical γ-Doradus IS agrees well with the observed IS, except in the extended blue region. In terms of radial orders, our models consistently reproduce the excited modes in broad agreement with observations for l= 1, l= 2, and Rossby modes. We also show that the range of excited radial orders is strongly dependent on the effective temperature. The range of excited radial orders can be used to constrain the position of a star within the γ-Doradus IS and may provide insights into the physical mechanisms responsible for the discrepancies observed in the blue region. All computed grids are made available and include mode damping and growth rates for γ-Doradus stars, obtained with a time-dependent treatment of the convection-oscillation interaction.

AI.tldr: This study systematically explores the theoretical γ-Doradus instability strip using stellar models with varying masses (1.35–2.5 M☉), metallicities (Z=0.01–0.025), and solid-body rotation rates (Ω=0–0.5 Ω_crit), finding broad agreement with observations except for the extended blue region, and provides the full grid of models with oscillation parameters including mode damping/growth rates.
AI.motivation: Despite Kepler providing large-scale observations of γ-Doradus stars, no systematic study has explored the effects of different physical processes (rotation, metallicity) on the γ-Doradus instability strip, and there is a persistent limitation in predicting the blue edge where many observed stars reside.
AI.method: Non-adiabatic pulsation computations were performed on a grid of stellar models spanning masses 1.35–2.5 M☉, metallicities Z=0.01–0.025, and solid-body rotation rates up to 0.5 Ω_crit, using a time-dependent treatment of convection–oscillation interaction to obtain mode damping and growth rates.
AI.result: The theoretical γ-Doradus instability strip agrees well with observations except in the extended blue region. Excited modes for l=1, l=2, and Rossby modes are reproduced in broad agreement with observations. The range of excited radial orders strongly depends on effective temperature and can be used to constrain a star's position within the instability strip and probe the physical mechanisms behind blue-edge discrepancies.
AI.conclusion: The full grid of models and oscillation parameters is made publicly available, providing a modern resource for the community and offering radial-order ranges as a diagnostic tool for placing stars within the γ-Doradus instability strip and understanding the blue-region discrepancy.

title: Search for magnetic fields in seven slowly rotating A stars
summary: A small fraction of A-type stars host strong fossil magnetic fields. Identifying them relies on indirect indicators such as chemical peculiarities, slow rotation, and rotational modulation, which are also shared by non-magnetic stars. Assessing their reliability is essential for future surveys. We magnetically characterise seven slowly rotating, chemically peculiar A-type stars selected through two complementary strategies. Three were selected from abundance analysis combined with potential intrinsically slow rotation, and four from a spectral depression at 5200 Angstrom combined with rotational modulation in TESS photometry. We obtained high-resolution spectropolarimetry, applied least squares deconvolution, and measured longitudinal field strengths for detections. For non-detections, we derived upper limits on polar field strength and evaluated the critical fields of Zahn and Spruit. We detect magnetic fields in all four stars selected via the spectral depression and photometric criterion, with longitudinal field strengths of approximately 145-2900 G, while none of the three stars selected via abundance and slow rotation shows a Zeeman signature. Combined upper limits for two non-detections lie below or near the magnetic desert boundary, but only one is also below the critical fields required for rigid rotation. The non-detections are most naturally interpreted as Am stars. Among the detections, HD 63843 stands out as a magnetic $δ$ Scuti pulsator, promising for magneto-asteroseismology. In conclusion, slow rotation combined with chemical peculiarity alone does not reliably trace large scale magnetic fields, whereas adding the 5200 Angstrom depression and stable rotational modulation in space photometry appears to select magnetic A-type stars with high efficiency, providing a practical guideline for future spectropolarimetric surveys.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates two selection strategies for identifying magnetic A-type stars via spectropolarimetry: abundance analysis plus slow rotation, and a 5200 Å depression plus rotational modulation in TESS photometry. Magnetic fields were detected in all four stars from the latter strategy (145-2900 G) but in none of the three from the former, showing that the 5200 Å/photometric criteria are highly efficient while abundance+slow-rotation alone is unreliable.
AI.motivation: A small fraction of A-type stars host strong fossil magnetic fields, but identifying them relies on indirect indicators (chemical peculiarity, slow rotation, rotational modulation) that are shared by non-magnetic stars. Assessing the reliability of these indicators is essential for planning future large-scale spectropolarimetric surveys.
AI.method: Seven slowly rotating, chemically peculiar A-type stars were selected: three via abundance analysis with presumably intrinsic slow rotation, and four via a 5200 Å spectral depression combined with rotational modulation in TESS photometry. High-resolution spectropolarimetry with least squares deconvolution was used to measure longitudinal fields; for non-detections, upper limits on polar field strength and Zahn/Spruit critical fields were evaluated.
AI.result: All four stars selected via the 5200 Å depression + photometric modulation showed detected magnetic fields (longitudinal strengths ~145-2900 G), while none of the three selected via abundance + slow rotation showed Zeeman signatures. Combined upper limits for two non-detections lie below or near the magnetic desert boundary, but only one is also below critical fields for rigid rotation. The non-detections are best interpreted as Am stars. HD 63843 is a magnetic δ Scuti pulsator of interest for magneto-asteroseismology.
AI.conclusion: Slow rotation combined with chemical peculiarity alone is not a reliable tracer of large-scale magnetic fields. Combining the 5200 Å depression with stable rotational modulation in space photometry selects magnetic A-type stars with high efficiency, offering a practical guideline for future spectropolarimetric surveys.

title: Probing magnetic fields in stars: A 2D oscillation framework including rotation and magnetism
summary: Understanding the role of internal magnetic fields in stars remains a major challenge for the description of angular momentum transport and stellar evolution. It is therefore essential to probe these magnetic fields within the star, and asteroseismology provides a powerful means to do so. In this work, we present a new implementation of the 2D oscillation code ( ), which incorporates the effects of both stellar rotation and magnetic fields. Adaptive Code of Oscillations towards Realistic modeling The code has been rendered modular, making it possible to specify the set of equations to solve and the assumptions through a symbolic calculus approach. The full set of adiabatic, non-radial pulsation equations is solved using a spectral approach for the angular part of the modes and high-order finite differences for the radial part. As a first step, we focus on a magnetic field that is purely toroidal and axisymmetric about the star's rotation axis. The numerical results are compared against first-order perturbative predictions in the weak-field regime and with the traditional approximation of rotation and magnetism (TARM) in the case of stronger magnetic fields. We validate this new implementation of against perturbative and TARM approaches, showing good agreement and demonstrating the robustness of the code. The breakdown of these methods provides general validity limits. We show that internal magnetic fields leave signatures in the period spacing of g modes. These features provide a promising seismic diagnostic to probe deep stellar magnetism in γ Dor stars. Future work will aim to extend this framework to more realistic magnetic field topologies and a broader range of pulsating stars, including red giants.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a new modular implementation of the 2D oscillation code ACOR (Adaptive Code of Oscillations towards Realistic modeling) that incorporates both stellar rotation and internal magnetic fields, specifically testing it with purely toroidal, axisymmetric magnetic fields. The code is validated against perturbative predictions in the weak-field regime and the Traditional Approximation of Rotation and Magnetism (TARM) for stronger fields. The results demonstrate that internal magnetic fields leave detectable signatures in the period spacing of g modes, providing a promising seismic diagnostic for probing deep stellar magnetism in γ Dor stars.
AI.motivation: Understanding internal magnetic fields in stars is crucial for describing angular momentum transport and stellar evolution, yet probing these fields remains challenging. Asteroseismology offers a powerful observational window, but existing pulsation codes do not adequately incorporate the combined effects of rotation and magnetic fields.
AI.method: The authors present a new modular implementation of the 2D oscillation code ACOR, which uses a symbolic calculus approach to specify the set of equations and assumptions. The full adiabatic, non-radial pulsation equations are solved with a spectral method for the angular part and high-order finite differences for the radial part. For the initial test case, a purely toroidal, axisymmetric magnetic field aligned with the rotation axis is considered. The code is validated against first-order perturbative predictions (weak-field regime) and the Traditional Approximation of Rotation and Magnetism (TARM) for stronger magnetic fields.
AI.result: The new ACOR implementation shows good agreement with both perturbative and TARM approaches, demonstrating the robustness of the code. The breakdown of these approximate methods defines general validity limits. Internal magnetic fields are shown to leave characteristic signatures in the period spacing of g modes, which serves as a promising seismic diagnostic for deep stellar magnetism in γ Dor stars.
AI.conclusion: The validated ACOR code provides a new tool for probing internal stellar magnetism through asteroseismology. The period-spacing signatures caused by magnetic fields in g modes offer a viable diagnostic for γ Dor stars. Future work will extend the framework to more realistic magnetic field topologies and a broader range of pulsating stars, including red giants.

title: On the Origin of a Dusty Circumstellar Medium around Red Supergiants
summary: Red supergiant (RSG) stars are widely recognized as significant sources of dust, enriching the interstellar medium. However, the physical conditions that regulate dust nucleation in their winds remain poorly constrained. We investigate the formation of molecules and dust in RSG and explore how enhanced mass loss can produce a dense, dust-rich circumstellar medium (CSM) before core collapse. We couple time-dependent mass loss with non-equilibrium chemistry to model the formation of molecules and dust precursors using mass loss rates ranging from 10$^{-6}$ to 10$^{-2}$ \Mdot\ and both constant and accelerating wind profiles. Molecules such as CO, H$_2$O, SiO, HCN, CS, SO, NH$_3$, H$_2$, and O$_2$ form efficiently in the CSM, with masses varying between 10$^{-15}$--10$^{-2}$ \Ms. O-rich dust, namely silicates and alumina, dominates the dust composition. The total dust mass ranges between 10$^{-8}$ and 3$\times$10$^{-3}$ \Ms. Accelerated winds produce more dust and allow dust formation closer to the stellar surface. The resulting fluxes exhibit strong mid-infrared excesses. The 9.7 and 18 \mic\ silicate features appear in either emission or absorption depending on the optical depth of the circumstellar medium. The time-dependent mass-loss history of our SN~2023ixf progenitor models results in a gradual increase in CSM dust mass toward explosion. A clumpy CSM provides a substantially better match to the observed optical and infrared fluxes, demonstrating the importance of time-dependent mass loss, CSM structure, and wind acceleration in shaping the observable properties of red supergiant progenitors.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates molecule and dust formation in red supergiant (RSG) winds by coupling time-dependent mass loss with non-equilibrium chemistry. Using mass loss rates from 10^-6 to 10^-2 Mdot and constant/accelerating wind profiles, they find efficient formation of molecules like CO, H2O, SiO, and O-rich dust (silicates, alumina). Accelerated winds produce more dust closer to the stellar surface, yielding strong mid-infrared excesses. Time-dependent mass loss in SN 2023ixf progenitor models produces gradually increasing CSM dust mass, and a clumpy CSM best matches observed fluxes.
AI.motivation: The physical conditions regulating dust nucleation in red supergiant (RSG) winds are poorly constrained, despite RSGs being significant dust sources that enrich the interstellar medium. Understanding how enhanced mass loss can produce a dense, dust-rich circumstellar medium (CSM) before core collapse is crucial for interpreting observable properties of RSG progenitors.
AI.method: The authors couple time-dependent mass loss with non-equilibrium chemistry to model molecule and dust precursor formation in RSG winds. They explore mass loss rates ranging from 10^-6 to 10^-2 Mdot and consider both constant and accelerating wind profiles. They track the formation of various molecules and dust species, and apply the model to SN 2023ixf progenitor scenarios.
AI.result: Molecules (CO, H2O, SiO, HCN, CS, SO, NH3, H2, O2) form efficiently with masses from 10^-15 to 10^-2 Msun. O-rich dust (silicates and alumina) dominates, with total dust masses between 10^-8 and 3x10^-3 Msun. Accelerated winds produce more dust and enable dust formation closer to the stellar surface, causing strong mid-infrared excesses. The 9.7 and 18 micron silicate features appear in emission or absorption depending on CSM optical depth. Time-dependent mass loss in SN 2023ixf models yields a gradual increase in CSM dust toward explosion, and a clumpy CSM provides substantially better agreement with observed fluxes.
AI.conclusion: Time-dependent mass loss, CSM structure, and wind acceleration are crucial in shaping the observable properties of RSG progenitors. Clumpy CSM structures and accelerating winds significantly improve agreement with observations of SN 2023ixf, highlighting the importance of realistic mass-loss histories in modeling pre-supernova environments.

title: A high-frequency type II radio burst associated with an X2.3 class flare
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal, 18 Pages, 8 Figures, 1 Table
summary: Radio observations provide a powerful diagnostic of the solar corona, enabling investigations of dynamic phenomena associated with solar flares, coronal mass ejections (CMEs), and shock waves. We present a multiwavelength analysis of a rare high-frequency type II radio burst (starting frequency of $\sim$750 MHz and frequency drift rate of $\sim$0.5 MHz s$^{-1}$) associated with the X2.3-class solar flare that occurred on 6 November 2024. A propagating EUV disturbance was observed shortly after the flare onset in the SDO/AIA field of view, while radio spectrographs recorded the type II burst between 13:46 and 13:56 UT over a frequency range of $\sim$750 to 45 MHz. Radio imaging observations from the Nançay Radioheliograph (NRH) show that the radio sources propagate southward during the event. X-ray spectroscopy from HEL1OS onboard Aditya-L1 and imaging observations from STIX onboard Solar Orbiter reveal signatures of efficient non-thermal electron acceleration associated with the flare. An NLFFF extrapolation identifies a pre-eruptive magnetic flux rope in the source region, while white-light coronagraph observations obtained during the event show no detectable large-scale CME. The speed of the erupting flux rope, derived from stereoscopic EUV observations, is consistent, within measurement uncertainties, with the shock speed inferred from the radio dynamic spectrum. Together, these observations suggest that compact flux rope eruptions, even in the absence of a detectable white-light CME, can generate low-coronal shocks capable of producing high-frequency type II radio emission.

AI.tldr: A multiwavelength study of a rare high-frequency type II radio burst (starting ~750 MHz) associated with an X2.3 solar flare on 6 Nov 2024, showing that a compact, stealth-like flux rope eruption—even without a detectable white-light CME—can generate low-coronal shocks producing high-frequency type II radio emission.
AI.motivation: High-frequency type II radio bursts are rare and poorly understood. This study aims to determine how such bursts can be produced, especially when no large-scale CME is observed, by combining multi-instrument observations to constrain the shock driver.
AI.method: Multiwavelength analysis combining radio dynamic spectra, NRH radio imaging, SDO/AIA EUV observations, HEL1OS X-ray spectroscopy, STIX imaging, NLFFF extrapolation for magnetic flux rope identification, stereoscopic EUV-derived eruption speed, and white-light coronagraph data.
AI.result: The type II burst drifted from ~750 to 45 MHz; radio sources propagated southward; strong non-thermal electron acceleration was observed; NLFFF revealed a pre-eruptive flux rope; no white-light CME was detected; the eruption speed matched the shock speed within uncertainties.
AI.conclusion: Compact flux rope eruptions lacking detectable white-light CME signatures can still drive low-coronal shocks capable of generating high-frequency type II radio emission.

title: An All-Sky Catalog of 6.5 Million Primary Red Clump Stars from Gaia DR3 XP Spectra
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Catalogs available at https://nadc.china-vo.org/res/r101871/
summary: Red clump (RC) stars are excellent standard candles for mapping the three-dimensional structure of the Milky Way. We construct an all-sky catalog of 6.5 million primary RC stars using spectroscopic estimates of asteroseismic parameters inferred from Gaia DR3 low-resolution XP spectra. We train a mixture density network (MDN) on a cross-matched sample. The network maps each 343-dimensional corrected XP spectrum to estimates of $ΔΠ_{1}$, the asymptotic period spacing of dipole gravity modes, and $Δν$, the large frequency separation. We select primary RC stars using these two estimates. We release two complementary catalogs defined by different parameter-space cuts and thresholds: a high-purity Tier 1 sample of 532,189 stars with 97% purity and a high-completeness Tier 2 sample of 6,534,931 stars with 86% completeness. Both catalogs cover the full celestial sphere. We provide distances and extinction values for all stars. We obtain a median photometric distance precision of 6% for Tier 1 RC stars. Using the resultant distances, we independently calibrate the Gaia DR3 parallax zero-point offset. The three-dimensional density distribution traced by the Tier 2 sample extends continuously to $R\approx25$ kpc. Both catalogs are publicly available. These catalogs provide a valuable resource for Galactic archaeology, delivering a homogeneous dataset to trace the chemo-dynamical evolution of the Milky Way and to calibrate models of stellar populations.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs an all-sky catalog of ~6.5 million primary red clump stars using a mixture density network trained on Gaia DR3 XP spectra to infer asteroseismic parameters (ΔΠ₁ and Δν). Two catalogs are released: a high-purity Tier 1 (532,189 stars, 97% purity) and a high-completeness Tier 2 (6.5 million, 86% completeness). Distances and extinction values are provided with 6% median photometric distance precision for Tier 1. The distances enable an independent calibration of the Gaia DR3 parallax zero-point offset, and the 3D density distribution extends continuously to R≈25 kpc.
AI.motivation: Red clump stars are ideal standard candles for mapping the Milky Way's 3D structure, but traditional identification methods are limited in scale and completeness. The motivation is to construct a large, homogeneous all-sky catalog of primary RC stars to enable Galactic archaeology and trace the chemo-dynamical evolution of the Milky Way.
AI.method: A mixture density network (MDN) is trained on a cross-matched sample (Gaia DR3 with seismic data) to map 343-dimensional corrected XP spectra to estimates of the asymptotic period spacing of dipole gravity modes (ΔΠ₁) and the large frequency separation (Δν). These two estimates are used to select primary RC stars, producing two catalogs defined by different parameter-space cuts and thresholds. Distances and extinction values are computed, and the resultant distances are used to calibrate the Gaia DR3 parallax zero-point offset.
AI.result: The method yields 532,189 high-purity RC stars (97% purity) in Tier 1 and 6,534,931 high-completeness RC stars (86% completeness) in Tier 2, both covering the full celestial sphere. Median photometric distance precision is 6% for Tier 1. The 3D density distribution traced by Tier 2 extends continuously to R≈25 kpc, and independent Gaia DR3 parallax zero-point calibration is achieved.
AI.conclusion: The two publicly available catalogs provide a large, homogeneous dataset of primary red clump stars spanning the full sky to R≈25 kpc, serving as a valuable resource for Galactic archaeology, chemo-dynamical studies of the Milky Way, and calibration of stellar population models.
